name: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1865 (Treaty of the Little Arkansas)
promises: Article 2 set apart a reservation between the Arkansas and Cimarron rivers for the nations' 'absolute and undisturbed use and occupation'. The Senate amended it so that the President, with the tribes' assent, would designate a reservation with no part in Kansas.
Article 3: until they moved to the reservation, the nations could live and range freely over the unsettled country between the Arkansas and Platte rivers.

Article 6: as reparation for the Sand Creek massacre of November 29, 1864, 320 acres to each of four named chiefs, 160 acres to each person widowed or orphaned there, and payment for property destroyed or taken by the troops.
Article 7: yearly spending for forty years of $20 a person before removal and $40 a person after it.
Article 4: compensation, as Congress judged just, for injury caused by any roads or military posts built on the reservation.

breaches.what: The National Park Service, in an interpretive history page, writes that in Article 6 the government effectively assumed responsibility for the Sand Creek massacre by committing to compensate those who lost property there, and that reparations to many other descendants have never been paid.
breaches.whoFoundIt: National Park Service, 'Sand Creek Massacre: Legacies' timeline
breaches.quote: Reparations to many other descendants have never been paid.

breaches.what: Descendants of Sand Creek survivors sued for an accounting of the Article 6 reparations and the $39,050 Congress appropriated for them in 1866. The Tenth Circuit described the event as ignominious but affirmed dismissal because the United States had not waived its sovereign immunity; it did not decide whether the reparations were paid.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Flute v. United States, No. 14-1405 (10th Cir. 2015)
breaches.quote: This case arises out of an ignominious event in the history of this Nation.

breaches.what: Steve Brady, co-chair of the Northern Cheyenne Sand Creek Massacre Site Committee, told a House committee that Article 6 admits US responsibility and promises reparations, and that the Indian Claims Commission refused to hear it as a tribal claim, saying descendants would have to bring it.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Testimony of Steve Brady, Northern Cheyenne Sand Creek Massacre Site Committee, House Committee on Resources

breaches.what: The Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho land claims arising from this cession and those of 1861 and 1867 were settled by a $15,000,000 compromise in Dockets 329-A and 329-B, without a finding on whether the price paid was unconscionable.

landTaken: By Article 2 the nations relinquished all claims outside the new reservation, including the country between the forks of the Platte, the Rocky Mountains and the Arkansas. The Indian Claims Commission valued the whole 1851 Cheyenne and Arapaho territory, 51,210,000 acres, at $23,500,000 as of October 14, 1865, the date the parties agreed the United States acquired it (16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162).
compensation: Congress appropriated $39,050 in 1866 for those who suffered at Sand Creek (as recited in Flute v. United States). The Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho accepted a $15,000,000 compromise of their land claims in 1965.
today: The Article 2 reservation was never occupied: the ICC found the Senate amendment required a substitute reservation, which the Medicine Lodge treaty of 1867 provided, and that treaty in turn was replaced by the 1869 executive-order reservation in Oklahoma. As of the 2015 Flute ruling, no court had ordered an accounting of the Article 6 reparations.

openQuestions: Article 6 is itself a government admission that the massacre happened while the people were at peace and under promised protection. It is a promise made in this treaty, not a breach of it, so it is listed as a promise here; whether it is a breach of Article 4 of the 1861 treaty (kappler-815) is discussed in that file.

Assent to the Senate amendments: the proclamation printed in H. Ex. Doc. 104 (1868) records the Arapaho and Cheyenne chiefs assenting on November 10, 1866, at Fort Zarah, and the Apache on November 19, 1866. Whether a reservation was then designated under the amended Article 2 is covered by the ICC findings in Docket 329.
The Flute opinion's account that funds went partly to the tribes and that unspent money returned to surplus in 1872 is the plaintiffs' allegation, not a finding, and is left out of the breaches.
No Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes (Oklahoma) page on this treaty was found.

Audit 2026-11-08: the National Park Service entry changed from government-admission to historian. An NPS interpretive page is a historian source, not a formal admission by the United States. With no court, Commission, statute or formal admission finding left, the status falls from broken to contested. A formal finding that the Article 6 reparations were not paid (for example a congressional report or the 1866 appropriation's accounting) would restore it.

Search 2026-11-08 for a formal finding that the Article 6 reparations were not paid or the lands never granted, none found: (1) ICC Cheyenne-Arapaho decisions in Dockets 329, 329-A, 329-B and 348 (pointers 110, 30, 242, 304, 412, 2123, 2414, 1020, 959, 1119) do not mention Sand Creek or Article 6 reparations; (2) Public Law 106-465 (2000) findings describe the massacre but say nothing of reparations; (3) Senate Report 106-418 (2000) says victims "received minor compensation" under the treaty and that "little was actually done", which records partial payment rather than non-payment, and Senate Reports 108-323 and 109-20 repeat that minor compensation was provided; (4) H. Ex. Doc. 104 (1868) concerns surveys for the Article 5 grants to relatives by blood, not the Article 6 grants; (5) the NPS timeline page also says the reparations were never paid, but it is the same interpretive kind of source as the Legacies page. Not reached: Commissioner of Indian Affairs annual reports 1866 to 1872 (not loaded as text), the accounting of the 1866 $39,050 appropriation, and any 1870s to 1890s Serial Set document on the Article 6 selections; these are the leads for restoring broken.

plain.promised: A reservation between the Arkansas and Cimarron rivers, yearly spending for forty years, and, as reparation for the Sand Creek massacre, land for survivors and payment for property the troops destroyed or took.
plain.happened: The National Park Service writes that reparations to many descendants have never been paid. No formal finding of breach has been located: in 2015 an appeals court dismissed the descendants' suit on sovereign immunity without deciding whether they were paid.
plain.today: Congress appropriated $39,050 in 1866 for those who suffered at Sand Creek; as of 2015 no court had ordered an accounting. The land claims were settled by a $15,000,000 compromise in 1965. The reservation was never occupied.
